lesson_1.title: Brute Force: Finding the Biggest Number
task: A 'Brute Force' approach means checking every single item one by one to find the answer. Let's find the biggest number in a list by checking everything.
Instructions:
1. Open the 'Functions' tab and create a function named `find_max` with an input `arr`.
2. First, check if the list is empty using an 'If' block from the 'Logic' tab. If it is empty, return the text `'Error'`.
3. Open the 'Variables' tab and create a variable called `max_val`. Set it to the first item in the list (index 0).
4. Open the 'Loops' tab and use a 'for each item in list' block to check every number in `arr`.
5. Inside the loop, use an 'If' block: if the current item is greater than `max_val`, update `max_val` to that item.
6. Return `max_val` at the very end.

lesson_1.title: Brute Force: Finding the Smallest Number
task: Finding the minimum value is exactly like finding the maximum, except we flip our logic to look for the smallest number instead!
Instructions:
1. Create the function `find_min(arr)`.
2. Check if the list is empty, and return `'Error'` if it is.
3. Start a variable `min_val` and set it to the first item in `arr`.
4. Loop through every item in `arr`. Use a 'Logic' block to see if the item is *less than* (`<`) `min_val`. If it is, update `min_val`.
5. Return `min_val`.

lesson_1.title: Exhaustive Search: The Duplicate Detector
task: Exhaustive search is often utilized to compare elements within a dataset against one another.
Implement a brute-force algorithm to determine if an array contains any duplicate values by checking every possible pair.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `has_duplicates(arr)`.
2. Construct an outer loop with iterator `i` from 0 to the length of `arr` minus 1.
3. Construct an inner loop with iterator `j` starting at `i + 1` up to the length of `arr` minus 1.
4. Inside the inner loop, evaluate if `arr[i] == arr[j]`. If true, an exact duplicate exists! Return `True` immediately.
5. If all exhaustive loops complete without detecting a match, return `False`.

lesson_1.title: Counting Specific Numbers
task: Let's check every number and only count the ones that meet a specific rule. We want to find out how many 'even' numbers are in the list.
Instructions:
1. Create `count_evens(arr)`.
2. Create a variable called `count` and set it to 0.
3. Loop through `arr` using the 'for each item in list' block.
4. Inside the loop, use the 'modulo' block from the 'Math' tab to check if `item % 2 == 0` (this means it is even).
5. If it is, go to the 'Math' tab and use the 'modify variable' block (like `count += 1`) to add 1 to `count`.
6. Return the `count` variable.
Sample Outputs:
count_evens([2, 4, 6, 8]) → 4
count_evens([1, 3, 5]) → 0

lesson_1.title: Stopping Early
task: If you only need to find the *first* matching item, you can save time by stopping the loop immediately as soon as you find it!
Instructions:
1. Create `first_negative(arr)`.
2. Start a loop through `arr`.
3. Use a 'Logic' block to check if the item is less than 0 (`item < 0`).
4. If true, use the 'return' block from the 'Functions' tab to immediately return the item. This stops the loop right away!
5. If the loop finishes and no negative number was found, return `0` at the bottom.
Sample Outputs:
first_negative([5, 3, -2, 8, -1]) → -2
first_negative([10, 20, 30]) → 0

lesson_2.title: Standard Linear Search
task: Linear Search is the most basic way to find something: you just check every single spot from start to finish until you spot the target.
Instructions:
1. Create `linear_search(arr, target)`.
2. Open the 'Loops' tab and use the 'count with i' loop. Set it to count from `0` to the length of the list minus `1`.
3. Inside, open the 'Logic' tab and check if the item at that index (`arr[i]`) equals the `target`.
4. If it does, return the index `i` immediately.
5. If you search the whole list and never find it, return `-1` at the end.

lesson_2.title: Counting Occurrences
task: Instead of stopping when we find the target, let's keep the loop going and count how many times it shows up in the whole list.
Instructions:
1. Create `count_occurrences(arr, target)`.
2. Create a variable `count` and set it to 0.
3. Use a 'for each item' loop to go through `arr`.
4. If the item equals the `target`, use the math modify block to add 1 to `count`.
5. Return the `count`.
Sample Outputs:
count_occurrences([5, 5, 5, 5], 5) → 4
count_occurrences([1, 2, 3], 4) → 0

lesson_2.title: Reverse Iteration: The Last Match
task: To find the LAST occurrence of a target, scanning the array from index 0 to the end is inefficient, as it forces the algorithm to check elements even after finding the target.
The optimal algorithmic approach is Reverse Iteration. By traversing from the back of the array to the front, the first match you encounter is mathematically guaranteed to be the last occurrence.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `last_occurrence(arr, target)`.
2. Construct a loop that iterates backwards. Set your iterator `i` to start at `len(arr) - 1`.
3. Set the loop to decrement (`-1`) down to `0`.
4. Inside the loop, evaluate `if arr[i] == target`. If true, execute an immediate `return i`.
5. Because we are moving backwards, this immediate return acts as an early-exit optimization.
6. If the loop concludes without finding a match, return `-1`.

lesson_2.title: Bounded Search with Validation
task: Algorithms often need to search within specific sub-sections of memory using dynamic pointers (`start` and `end`).
However, accepting dynamic bounds without validation is a critical stability risk. If `end` exceeds the array's actual boundaries, the program will crash.
Instructions:
1. Define `search_in_range(arr, target, start, end)`.
2. Defensive Validation 1: If `start < 0`, reset `start` to `0`.
3. Defensive Validation 2: If `end > len(arr) - 1`, clamp `end` to `len(arr) - 1`.
4. Now that your bounds are safe, construct a 'count with i' loop starting at your sanitized `start` value and stopping at your sanitized `end` value.
5. If `arr[i] == target`, return `i` immediately.
6. Return `-1` if the bounded search fails.

lesson_2.title: Saving All Matches
task: Let's find every single place a target appears and save those positions into a brand new list.
Instructions:
1. Create `multi_search(arr, target)`.
2. Open the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab and create an empty list called `results`.
3. Loop through every index `i` of `arr` using the 'count with i' loop.
4. If `arr[i] == target`, use the 'append to list' block to add `i` to your `results` list.
5. Return the `results` list.
Sample Outputs:
multi_search([2, 4, 6], 5) → []

lesson_3.title: Bubble Sort (Ascending)
task: Bubble Sort works by looking at two neighbors. If the left neighbor is bigger than the right neighbor, they swap places! You repeat this until the list is sorted.
Instructions:
1. Create `bubble_sort_asc(arr)`.
2. You'll need two loops. Make an outer 'count with i' loop that counts from 0 to the length of the list.
3. Make an inner 'count with j' loop that counts up to the length minus 1.

4. Check the neighbors: if `arr[j]` is greater than `arr[j+1]`, you need to swap them. Use your custom 'swap variable' block from the 'Variables' tab if needed, or do it manually with a temporary variable.
5. Return the sorted `arr`.
Sample Outputs:
bubble_sort_asc([9, 8, 7]) → [7, 8, 9]

lesson_3.title: Selection Sort: Pointer Tracking
task: Selection Sort works by dividing the array into a 'sorted' left side and an 'unsorted' right side. It exhaustively scans the unsorted side to find the smallest element and swaps it into place.
To do this, we must use Pointer Indirection: tracking the mathematical INDEX of the smallest number, rather than the number itself.
Instructions:
1. Define `selection_sort(arr)`.
2. Create an outer loop `i` from 0 to `len(arr) - 1`. This pointer marks the end of our sorted section.
3. Inside the outer loop, initialize a variable `min_idx = i`. We will assume the first unsorted item is the smallest until proven otherwise.
4. Create an inner loop `j` from `i + 1` to `len(arr) - 1`. This loop scans the remaining unsorted items.
5. Inside the inner loop, evaluate: `if arr[j] < arr[min_idx]`. If true, update our pointer: `min_idx = j`.
6. Once the inner loop finishes, `min_idx` holds the exact location of the smallest number. Swap it with our current starting position: `arr[i], arr[min_idx] = arr[min_idx], arr[i]`.
7. Return the sorted `arr`.

lesson_3.title: Bubble Sort (Descending)
task: To sort things from biggest to smallest, we just use the exact same Bubble Sort but flip our logic! If the left neighbor is *smaller*, swap them.
Instructions:
1. Create `bubble_sort_desc(arr)`.
2. Rebuild the two nested loops exactly like you did in the first Bubble Sort task.
3. Change your 'Logic' block comparison: if `arr[j]` is *less than* (`<`) `arr[j+1]`, execute the swap.
4. Return the `arr`.
Sample Outputs:
bubble_sort_desc([1, 2, 3]) → [3, 2, 1]

lesson_3.title: Selection Sort (Descending)
task: We can also flip Selection Sort. Instead of scanning for the smallest number, let's scan for the biggest number and pull it to the front.
Instructions:
1. Create `selection_sort_desc(arr)`.
2. Rebuild the nested loops from the first Selection Sort task. Initialize a `max_idx` tracker instead of a min tracker.
3. Change the comparison: if `arr[j] > arr[max_idx]`, update `max_idx`.
4. Swap the items at `i` and `max_idx`.
5. Return the array.
Sample Outputs:
selection_sort_desc([1, 2, 3]) → [3, 2, 1]
selection_sort_desc([10, 50, 20]) → [50, 20, 10]

lesson_3.title: A Single Bubble Pass
task: To really understand Bubble Sort, let's see what happens if we only run the inner loop exactly once. It will push the absolute biggest number all the way to the right!
Instructions:
1. Create `single_pass(arr)`.
2. Only make ONE 'count with j' loop that goes through the list up to the length minus 1.
3. If `arr[j] > arr[j+1]`, swap them.
4. Return the list. Because there's only one loop, this is much faster!

optimizations.title: Optimization Challenge: The Two-Pointer Squeeze
task: Checking every pair of numbers with nested loops to find a target sum takes O(n²) time.
If we are guaranteed that the array is strictly SORTED, we can completely eliminate the nested loops and find the target in O(n) time using converging pointers.
Optimization Guidelines:
1. Remove your nested loops. Initialize two variables: `left = 0`, and `right = len(arr) - 1`.
2. Construct a single `while` loop that runs continuously as long as `left < right`.
3. Inside the loop, calculate the `current_sum = arr[left] + arr[right]`.
4. If `current_sum == target`, return the array `[arr[left], arr[right]]`.
5. The Logic: If `current_sum < target`, we require a larger value to reach the target. Because the array is sorted, we move the left pointer up (`left = left + 1`).
6. If `current_sum > target`, we require a smaller value. Move the right pointer down (`right = right - 1`).
7. Return an empty list `[]` if the loops cross without finding a match.

optimizations.title: Optimization Challenge: The Sorted Majority
task: Your previous brute-force algorithm used nested loops to find the Majority Element, resulting in an O(n²) time complexity.
If you are informed that the input array is strictly SORTED, you can optimize this search down to an instantaneous O(1) time!
Optimization Guidelines:
1. Delete all of your loop blocks. We do not need to iterate!
2. By mathematical definition, if an element makes up more than half of a sorted array, it MUST overlap the exact center index.
3. Calculate the middle index: `mid = len(arr) // 2` (Use integer division).
4. Simply access and return the element at that exact index: `return arr[mid]`.
5. You have just optimized an exhaustive search into a constant-time lookup!

optimizations.title: Optimization Challenge: Fast Duplicate Detection
task: In a standard brute-force approach, checking every possible pair for duplicates requires nested loops, resulting in a sluggish O(n²) Time Complexity.
We can mathematically optimize this to O(n log n). By sorting the array first, any identical values are forced to sit right next to each other, allowing us to find them in a single scan!
Optimization Guidelines:
1. Open your nested-loop brute force code and delete both loops entirely.
2. First, sort the array in-place using the built-in sort command. (This operation costs O(n log n) time).
3. Now, create a single standard loop `i` iterating from `0` to `len(arr) - 2`. (We must stop at length minus 2 so we can safely peek ahead without causing an Index Out of Bounds error).
4. Inside the loop, evaluate adjacency: `if arr[i] == arr[i+1]`.
5. If a match is verified, execute `return True` immediately.
6. If the single linear scan completes with no matches, return `False`.
7. You have officially upgraded the algorithm's asymptotic class!
